meta.title: Deployment Patterns for AI Apps
meta.thesis: Deploying an AI app means choosing how the model is served, fronting it with a gateway, and placing yourself deliberately on the latency/throughput/cost tradeoff so it survives real load.

modules.title: Why deployment is its own problem
modules.sub: Starts the spine: the gap between a model that runs and a model that serves.
modules.summary: A model that returns one prediction in a notebook is not a deployed app. This module frames what changes when real users, concurrency, and uptime enter the picture — and why that demands deliberate deployment patterns.
objectives: Explain why running a model and serving a model are different problems.
Name the three things production traffic adds that a notebook never tests.
Identify the first tradeoff every deployment forces: latency versus cost.

blocks.title: Why a model that runs isn't a model that's deployed
blocks.analogy: A model in a notebook is a home-cooked meal; deploying it is opening a restaurant — the recipe is the easy part, surviving the dinner rush is the job.

spans.text: Before reading on, predict:
your model gives a great answer in a notebook in 200 ms. What three new problems appear the moment 500 users hit it at once?
In a notebook you call the model once and read the result. Nothing competes for the
gpu
, nothing fails halfway, and there is no "how many requests per second" to worry about. A deployed app has to answer for all of that.
Deployment patterns
exist precisely because the gap between "it works for me" and "it works for everyone" is where AI apps break.
Production traffic adds three things a single notebook call never tests:

items.text: Concurrency
— many requests arrive at once and contend for the same GPU.
Variability
— traffic spikes, prompts vary in length, and
latency
stops being a single number.
Failure
— a node dies, a queue overflows, or a new model version ships a regression.

spans.text: The first tradeoff you will meet over and over: making each answer faster usually means keeping expensive GPUs warm, while keeping cost low usually means accepting more
latency
. You cannot escape it — you can only place yourself on it deliberately.

blocks.title: Click through one production request
blocks.caption: What happens to a single inference request once your model is deployed — not just 'call model, get answer'.

steps.label: Request arrives
steps.detail: A client sends a prompt to your public endpoint. It hits the gateway first, not the model.

steps.label: Route & queue
steps.detail: The gateway authenticates, rate-limits, and routes to a serving replica — queuing if all GPUs are busy.

steps.label: GPU inference
steps.detail: The serving engine batches the request with others and runs it on the GPU; this is where latency is spent.

steps.label: Stream back
steps.detail: Tokens stream back through the gateway to the client; meanwhile autoscaling watches the queue depth.

stops.label: Intuition
stops.note: Good enough to picture: request in, answer out, GPU in the middle.

stops.label: Working model
stops.note: Enough detail to predict where queuing and cold starts add latency.

stops.label: Operational rigor
stops.note: Adds batching, autoscaling, and the gateway's auth/rate-limit responsibilities.

blocks.title: How to frame any deployment decision

spans.text: Write one sentence: how many requests per second do you expect at peak, and how fast must each one come back? This single number shapes every later choice.
Decide which matters more for THIS app: tail
latency
(a user is waiting) or
throughput
per GPU-dollar (a batch job at 3am). You rarely get both.
Pick the one outage you most fear — a cold-start spike, a saturated queue, a bad model version — and make sure your design has an answer for it before you ship.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: the same model, two deployments

spans.text: Team A serves a chat assistant: users wait on every token, so they keep two GPUs warm and optimize tail
latency
. The GPUs sit half-idle, but answers feel instant.
Team B runs the same model to summarize a million documents overnight. Nobody is waiting, so they pack requests into large batches for maximum
throughput
per dollar and let any single job take seconds. Same weights, opposite deployment — because the load is different.

blocks.title: Technical note: latency is a distribution, not a number

spans.text: In production you never report "average latency" alone — you track percentiles (p50, p95, p99). A model with a great average can still have a p99 that times out for one user in a hundred, and that user is the one who complains.
Set your latency target as a percentile under a stated load, e.g. 'p95 under 800 ms at 50 requests/second' — a number you can actually test against.

blocks.prompt: What is the core reason deploying an AI model is harder than calling it in a notebook?

options.text: Deployed models use different weights than notebook models.
Production adds concurrency, traffic variability, and failure — none of which a single call tests.
Notebooks cannot run on a GPU.

blocks.explanation: The weights are identical. What changes is the environment: many concurrent requests, spiky load, and the need to survive failures — which is exactly what deployment patterns address.

modules.title: How serving actually works
modules.sub: Follows module 1: open up the request path you just framed.
modules.summary: Now that you know production load is the problem, this module traces the request path and names the three layers — gateway, serving engine, GPU — that every AI deployment is built from.
objectives: Trace an inference request through gateway, serving engine, and GPU.
Explain what each layer owns and why batching lives in the serving engine.
Identify which layer to inspect first when latency or errors spike.

spans.text: Before reading on, recall from module 1:
what were the three things production traffic adds that a single notebook call never tests?
(Concurrency, traffic variability, and failure.) The three layers below exist to absorb exactly those three pressures — keep that mapping in mind as you read.

blocks.title: The three layers of every AI deployment
blocks.analogy: Like a restaurant: the gateway is the host who seats and paces guests, the serving engine is the line cook batching tickets, and the GPU is the single hot stove everything competes for.

spans.text: Almost every AI deployment, however fancy, is three layers stacked in front of the model weights.

items.text: Gateway
— the public front door. It authenticates callers, enforces rate limits, and routes each request to a healthy replica. It owns nothing about the model itself.
Serving
engine — the process that holds the loaded model and turns a request into tokens. It batches concurrent requests together so the GPU stays busy.
GPU
— the scarce, expensive hardware that does the actual matrix math. Everything above exists to keep this one resource fed and never idle.

spans.text: The key insight:
batching lives in the serving engine, not the gateway
. The engine waits a few milliseconds to gather several requests, runs them through the GPU in one pass, and so trades a little
latency
for much higher
throughput
. That single decision is the heart of AI serving.

blocks.title: Follow one request through the layers

spans.text: The request hits the
gateway
first: it verifies the API key, checks the caller is under their rate limit, and picks a serving replica that is alive and not overloaded.
The
serving
engine groups your request with other in-flight ones and schedules them onto the GPU together, so the hardware processes many sequences per pass.
The
gpu
runs the forward passes; tokens stream back up through the gateway to the client. Time spent here is most of your
latency

blocks.title: Concrete use case: where does the latency go?

spans.text: A user reports a 4-second response. Knowing the three layers tells you exactly where to look: was the request queued at the
gateway
because every replica was busy (a scaling problem), did it wait in the
serving
engine's batch window (a batching-config problem), or was the
gpu
genuinely slow on a long prompt (a model/hardware problem)?
Without the layered model you guess. With it, you instrument each boundary and the 4 seconds resolves into 'queued for 3.5s' — and now you know to add capacity, not a faster GPU.

blocks.title: Technical note: why batching changes everything

spans.text: GPUs are massively parallel but have high fixed cost per kernel launch. Running one request at a time leaves most of the chip idle. Continuous batching (as in vLLM) keeps slotting new requests into the running batch as others finish, pushing
throughput
several-fold higher at the cost of a small, bounded wait.
When you tune a serving engine, the two dials that matter most are max batch size and max wait time — they directly trade latency for throughput.

blocks.prompt: In an AI serving stack, which layer is responsible for batching concurrent requests together?

options.text: The gateway, because it sees all incoming traffic.
The serving engine, because it holds the model and schedules work onto the GPU.
The GPU driver, automatically.

blocks.explanation: The gateway authenticates and routes; the GPU does math. Batching — deciding which requests run together — lives in the serving engine, which is where the latency/throughput trade is made.

modules.title: Choosing a deployment pattern
modules.sub: Follows module 2: with the layers clear, pick how to run them.
modules.summary: With the request path understood, this module is the central decision: which deployment pattern fits your app. Each pattern places you differently on the latency, throughput, cost, and operational-burden tradeoff.
objectives: Distinguish real-time, batch, and serverless serving patterns.
Weigh self-hosted versus managed inference against cost and control.
Choose the smallest pattern that meets your latency and load target.

blocks.title: The patterns you actually choose between
blocks.analogy: Real-time is a drive-through (fast, one car at a time, costly to keep open); batch is a catering kitchen (cook everything at once, cheap per plate, nobody waiting); serverless is a pop-up that appears only when a customer arrives (no idle cost, slow first plate).

spans.text: Once you know the layers, deployment becomes a small set of recurring patterns. Three cover most cases.

items.text: Real-time serving
— a warm endpoint answers each request as it arrives. Lowest
latency
, highest idle cost. Use for interactive apps.
Batch / offline
— collect inputs and run them in big batches when convenient. Best
throughput
per GPU-dollar, no one waiting. Use for bulk jobs.
Serverless / scale-to-zero
— spin a
gpu
up on demand, pay nothing when idle, but eat a cold-start delay on the first request. Use for spiky or low-volume traffic.

spans.text: Cutting across all three is a second axis:
self-hosted versus managed
. Self-hosting your own
serving
engine gives full control and lower per-token cost at scale, but you own the GPUs, patches, and pager. A managed API trades that control for someone else carrying the operational weight.

blocks.title: How to pick a pattern

spans.text: If a human is staring at a spinner, you need real-time serving and must optimize
latency
. If it is an offline job, batch wins on cost.
Steady high volume justifies always-warm GPUs. Spiky or rare traffic makes scale-to-zero attractive — you stop paying for idle
gpu
time, accepting a cold start.

steps.label: Do you have the ops capacity?

spans.text: Before choosing self-hosted, ask honestly: can your team run a
serving
engine on GPUs at 3am? If not, a managed endpoint is the smaller, safer choice until volume forces the move.

blocks.title: Real-time vs batch vs serverless

options.name: Real-time serving

cells.text: Lowest — endpoint stays warm, no cold start.
Poor at low traffic — you pay for idle GPUs.
Needs autoscaling, health checks, and monitoring.

options.whenToUse: Use when a human is waiting on the response (chat, search, assistants).

options.name: Batch / offline

cells.text: Irrelevant — jobs finish minutes to hours later.
Best — large batches keep the GPU fully utilized.
Simple — a queue and a worker, no uptime SLA.

options.whenToUse: Use for bulk processing where no user is waiting (nightly summaries, embeddings).

options.name: Serverless / scale-to-zero

cells.text: Good when warm, but cold starts add seconds.
Excellent for spiky traffic — zero idle cost.
Platform handles scaling; you tune cold-start behavior.

options.whenToUse: Use for low-volume or bursty traffic where idle cost would dominate.

blocks.howToRead: Pick the smallest pattern whose latency column meets your user requirement. If nobody is waiting, batch almost always wins on cost.

blocks.title: Technical note: the hidden cost of scale-to-zero

spans.text: A serverless GPU endpoint must load multi-gigabyte model weights into VRAM before it can answer. That cold start can take 10–60 seconds. The fix is not 'never use serverless' — it is keeping a small warm pool, or accepting cold starts only on traffic that tolerates them.
Measure cold-start time for YOUR model before committing to scale-to-zero — a 30-second first request is fine for a batch trigger and unacceptable for a chat UI.

blocks.prompt: You need to generate embeddings for 5 million documents overnight; no user is waiting. Which pattern fits best?

options.text: Real-time serving, for the lowest latency.
Batch / offline, for the best throughput per GPU-dollar.
A larger GPU, regardless of pattern.

blocks.explanation: Latency doesn't matter when nobody is waiting, so you optimize cost. Large batches keep the GPU fully utilized, giving the best throughput per dollar — exactly what batch serving is for.

modules.decisionItForces: Choose the deployment pattern for your AI app: real-time serving, batch/offline, or serverless scale-to-zero.

modules.title: A minimal serving setup
modules.sub: Follows module 3: turn the chosen pattern into a runnable artifact.
modules.summary: With a pattern chosen, this module sketches the smallest real-time serving endpoint and the autoscaling rule that protects the GPU. It is the worked-to-completion ramp: read the endpoint, then predict the missing scaling logic.
objectives: Read a minimal real-time serving endpoint and name what each part does.
Explain the autoscaling rule that decides when to add or drop a replica.
Verify an AI-generated serving config before trusting it in production.

blocks.title: The two pieces of a real-time endpoint
blocks.analogy: Like opening the restaurant on day one: you need one cook taking orders (the endpoint) and a rule for when to phone a second cook before the queue gets out of hand (autoscaling).

spans.text: A minimal real-time deployment is two pieces. First, a
serving
endpoint: a process that loads the model once, then answers requests on a port. Second, an
autoscaling rule
: logic that watches load and adds or removes replicas so the
gpu
is neither idle nor drowning.
The scaling signal that matters for AI serving is usually
queue depth
(requests waiting), not CPU. A GPU can sit at modest CPU while its request queue — and your
latency
— climbs.

blocks.title: Build it up one piece at a time

spans.text: Load weights into the
gpu
at startup, never per request — loading is the slow part, so do it once and reuse.
Accept a prompt, run inference, return tokens. This is the unit your
gateway
will route to and your autoscaler will replicate.
Watch queue depth: above a high-water mark, add a replica; below a low-water mark for a while, drop one. The code below leaves that rule for you to predict.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: a single warm endpoint

spans.text: Picture one GPU pod running a vLLM
serving
engine behind a
gateway
. At 10 requests/second it keeps p95
latency
under target. Traffic doubles at lunchtime; the queue grows, p95 creeps up, and the autoscaler spins a second pod — bringing latency back down without anyone paging an engineer.
That self-healing behavior is the whole point of pairing an endpoint with an autoscaling rule. The endpoint serves; the rule keeps it from falling over.

blocks.title: Completion problem: the autoscaling rule

spans.text: The endpoint loads the model once and answers requests; the autoscaler scales on queue depth, not CPU. Treat this as the smallest runnable shape — real deployments add health checks, timeouts, and metrics.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before you read should_scale: if queue_depth is 25 with 1 replica (high=20), what should it return — and why queue depth rather than CPU usage?
predictThenReveal.answer: It returns "up": 25 exceeds the high-water mark of 20, so a replica is added. Queue depth is the right signal because a GPU can show low CPU while requests pile up and latency climbs — CPU would never trigger the scale-up that latency actually needs.

syntax.explains: Loads weights into GPU memory once at startup so requests don't pay that cost.
How many requests are waiting — the load signal that tracks latency for GPU serving.
High- and low-water marks: thresholds that add a replica or remove one.

spans.text: If you let an AI assistant generate serving or autoscaling config, check these four things before trusting it — they are the ones models get wrong most often:

items.text: Is the model loaded once at startup, not inside the request handler? A per-request load silently kills throughput.
Does the autoscaler scale on queue depth or latency — not CPU? CPU-based rules under-scale GPU workloads.
Is there a max-replica cap and a request timeout? Without them a traffic spike can burn unbounded GPU spend or hang forever.
Does it pin the model version, so a redeploy can't silently swap weights? (More on this next module.)

blocks.prompt: For a GPU-backed real-time endpoint, which signal should the autoscaler watch?

options.text: CPU utilization, the standard web-server metric.
Request queue depth (or latency), because a GPU can be saturated while CPU stays low.
Total disk usage on the node.

blocks.explanation: GPU inference work doesn't show up as CPU load, so CPU-based autoscaling under-reacts. Queue depth (or measured latency) directly reflects whether the GPU is keeping up with demand.

modules.title: Hardening and knowing it works
modules.sub: Follows module 4: stress the setup you built and prove it survives.
modules.summary: The final module is the WHEN-IT-BREAKS step: the production failure modes that take AI deployments down, and the checks that prove a setup is ready. It ends by deciding how much rigor your app actually needs.
objectives: Name the three failure modes that cause most AI deployment outages.
Recall how the request path and autoscaling rule defend against each.
Decide the right level of deployment rigor for a given app.

spans.text: Before reading on, recall from module 4:
what signal did we say a GPU autoscaler should watch, and why not CPU?
(Queue depth or latency — a GPU can be saturated while CPU stays low.) Two of the failure modes below are exactly what happens when that defense is missing or mis-tuned.

blocks.title: How AI deployments break in practice
blocks.analogy: The grand-opening disasters: the kitchen is cold when the first guest arrives (cold start), tickets pile up faster than the cook can plate (queue overflow), and the menu on the counter isn't the one the kitchen is cooking (version skew).

spans.text: Knowing the happy path isn't enough. Three failure modes cause most AI deployment outages — recognize them and you defend against them.
1. Cold-start latency spikes
A scaled-to-zero or freshly-added replica must load weights into the
gpu
before it can answer. The first requests hit a 10–60 second wall. Defense: a small warm pool, or pre-warming before predicted spikes.
2. Queue overflow under load
Traffic outruns capacity, the request queue grows unbounded, and
latency
climbs until requests time out. Defense: autoscale on queue depth (module 4), cap the queue, and shed load gracefully rather than hanging.
3. Version skew (the non-obvious one)

A redeploy swaps the model weights but a cached prompt template, tokenizer, or downstream parser still expects the old version. Outputs look plausible but are subtly wrong. Defense: pin and log the model
versioning
so every response is traceable to exact weights, and roll out behind a canary.

blocks.title: A pre-launch readiness check

spans.text: Drive traffic at your stated peak and confirm p95
latency
holds. If it doesn't, you found a queue-overflow risk before users did.

steps.label: Trigger a cold start on purpose

spans.text: Scale a replica from zero and time the first response. Decide whether that delay is acceptable for this app, or whether you need a warm pool.
Confirm every response can be tied to an exact model
versioning
tag, so a bad rollout can be caught and reverted fast.

blocks.title: How much deployment rigor does this app need?

options.name: Prototype (single endpoint)

cells.text: Great for a demo or to prove value fast.
High under real load; no defense against spikes.

options.whenToUse: Use while traffic is tiny and an outage costs nothing.

options.name: Production (autoscaled + monitored)

cells.text: Right when real users depend on uptime.
Low — defends against queue overflow and skew.

options.whenToUse: Use once the app is on the critical path for users.

options.name: Optimized (multi-region, tuned batching)

cells.text: Best only after a measured cost or latency bottleneck.
High — specialist tuning and more infra to run.
Low, but added complexity is its own risk source.

options.whenToUse: Use only after metrics prove the production tier is insufficient.

blocks.howToRead: Pick the smallest tier that meets your uptime and latency requirement. Jumping to 'optimized' before you have metrics adds risk without evidence.

blocks.title: Technical note: make every deployment observable

spans.text: The single habit that prevents most of these failures is observability: log the model
versioning
tag, queue depth, and per-percentile
latency
on every request. You cannot catch version skew or queue overflow you cannot see.
If a deployment claim would matter in a production review — 'p95 is under 800 ms', 'we're on model v3' — attach a metric or a log line that proves it.

blocks.prompt: A redeploy ships new weights, but responses are subtly wrong even though no error is thrown. Which failure mode is this?

options.text: Cold-start latency spike.
Version skew — a cached template, tokenizer, or parser still expects the old model.
Queue overflow.

blocks.explanation: No error plus plausible-but-wrong output is the signature of version skew. Pinning and logging the model version (and rolling out behind a canary) is how you catch and revert it fast.

modules.decisionItForces: Choose the right level of deployment rigor: prototype, production, or optimized — sized to the app's real uptime and latency needs.

gpu.label: GPU
gpu.laymanDefinition: The scarce, expensive parallel processor that runs the model's math — the resource every deployment is built to keep busy.
gpu.technicalNote: GPUs are massively parallel but costly per kernel launch, which is why serving engines batch requests to keep them fully utilized.

serving.label: Serving
serving.laymanDefinition: Running a trained model as a live service that answers requests, rather than calling it once in a script.
serving.technicalNote: The serving engine (e.g. vLLM) loads the model, batches concurrent requests, and schedules them onto the GPU.

gateway.label: Gateway
gateway.laymanDefinition: The public front door of a deployment: it authenticates callers, rate-limits, and routes requests to a healthy replica.
gateway.technicalNote: The gateway owns auth, rate limiting, and load balancing — not the model. It never runs inference itself.

latency.label: Latency
latency.laymanDefinition: How long one request takes to come back — reported as percentiles (p50, p95, p99), not a single average.
latency.technicalNote: Tail latency (p95/p99) under a stated load is the meaningful target; an average hides the slow requests users notice.

throughput.label: Throughput
throughput.laymanDefinition: How many requests the system handles per unit time — the dial you raise with batching, often at the cost of latency.
throughput.technicalNote: Higher batch sizes raise throughput per GPU-dollar but add a bounded wait, trading directly against latency.

versioning.label: Versioning
versioning.laymanDefinition: Tracking exactly which model weights produced each response, so a bad rollout can be traced and reverted.
versioning.technicalNote: Pin and log the model version end to end; mismatched template/tokenizer/weights cause silent version skew.

questions.prompt: A data scientist runs a model in a Jupyter notebook with no issues, then deploys it to production — and latency spikes, errors appear under load, and costs balloon. Which of the following best explains why deployment is its own problem, separate from running the model?

options.text: The model weights are too large to fit in a production server's memory.
Production traffic adds concurrency, variable load, and uptime requirements that a notebook never exercises.
Cloud GPUs use different floating-point precision than local machines.
Notebooks cache predictions, so they always appear faster than real serving.

questions.explanation: Production traffic introduces concurrent requests, unpredictable load spikes, and uptime pressure — none of which a single-user notebook ever tests.

questions.prompt: An inference request arrives at your deployed AI app. Tracing it through the stack: which layer is responsible for batching multiple requests together before they hit the GPU?

options.text: The API gateway, because it sees all incoming traffic first.
The GPU driver, because it schedules compute kernels.
The serving engine, because batching is an inference-optimization concern it owns.
The load balancer, because it distributes requests across replicas.

questions.explanation: The serving engine sits between the gateway and the GPU and owns inference-level optimizations like request batching to maximize GPU utilization.

questions.prompt: Your app scores millions of customer records overnight and results are needed by 6 AM — but no user is waiting in real time. Your GPU budget is tight. Which deployment pattern is the best fit?

options.text: Real-time serving with multiple always-on replicas.
Serverless scale-to-zero, triggered per request.
Batch / offline processing, scheduled to run during off-peak hours.
Self-hosted real-time endpoint with aggressive autoscaling.

questions.explanation: Batch/offline serving is purpose-built for high-volume, latency-tolerant workloads — it processes records in bulk on a schedule and avoids the cost of always-on infrastructure.

questions.prompt: Look at a minimal real-time serving config that defines a container image, a replica count, and an autoscaling rule (e.g., scale up when CPU/GPU utilization exceeds 70%, scale down when it drops below 30%). In one or two sentences, explain what the autoscaling rule is actually deciding and why both the scale-up AND scale-down thresholds matter.
questions.acceptableAnswer: The autoscaling rule decides when to add a new replica (to handle rising load without degrading latency) and when to remove one (to cut idle cost). Both thresholds matter because setting scale-up too high causes latency spikes under load, while setting scale-down too aggressively causes replicas to churn — spinning up and down repeatedly — which itself adds latency and cost.
questions.explanation: Autoscaling balances two opposing risks: under-provisioning (too few replicas → slow responses) and over-provisioning (too many idle replicas → wasted cost), so both thresholds need deliberate tuning.

questions.prompt: The three failure modes that cause most AI deployment outages are: GPU/memory exhaustion, a cascade of slow requests overwhelming the queue (request pile-up), and cold-start latency spikes. You're building an internal analytics tool used by ~10 people, with no SLA and results needed within a few minutes. What is the RIGHT level of deployment rigor?

options.text: Optimized — add quantization, multi-replica failover, and full observability to guard against all three failure modes.
Prototype — a single replica, no autoscaling, basic logging; the failure impact is low and the overhead of full hardening isn't justified.
Production — you still need request timeouts and at least two replicas to avoid any single point of failure.
Serverless only — cold starts are acceptable because users expect some delay.

questions.explanation: Deployment rigor should be sized to real uptime and latency needs — a low-traffic internal tool with no SLA warrants prototype-level setup, not the overhead of full production hardening.
